title: E-Government Survey 2026: Italia in crescita, +7 posizioni nella classifica mondiale
summary: E-Government Survey 2026: Italia in crescita, +7 posizioni nella classifica mondiale false glenda.gentili Mer, 11/25/2026 - 15:49 L'Italia migliora la propria posizione nel panorama globale della trasformazione digitale pubblica. È quanto emerge dalla 14ª edizione dell’E-Government Survey 2026, il rapporto biennale delle Nazioni Unite che monitora lo sviluppo dell’e-government nei Paesi membri attraverso l’E-Government Development Index (EGDI), l’indicatore che misura la maturità digitale delle amministrazioni pubbliche sulla base della qualità dei servizi online, delle infrastrutture digitali e del capitale umano.    Questa edizione assume un significato particolare: celebra infatti 25 anni di analisi globale confermandosi il principale punto di riferimento internazionale per valutare l’evoluzione dei governi digitali. Il rapporto, intitolato “From Digital Government to Agentic Government” , analizza 194 Paesi e descrive una fase di profonda trasformazione, caratterizzata anche dall’integrazione crescente dell’intelligenza artificiale nelle amministrazioni pubbliche. Nel 2026 ben 151 dei 194 Paesi valutati rientrano nelle fasce "alta" o "molto alta" dell'E-Government Development Index (EGDI) e il numero di Paesi che migliorano la propria collocazione supera di quattro volte quello dei Paesi che registrano un peggioramento.   Nuovi leader globali e centralità dell'Europa   La graduatoria 2026 vede la Repubblica di Corea al primo posto mondiale, seguita da Danimarca e Singapore. Completano la top ten Arabia Saudita, Emirati Arabi Uniti, Islanda, Regno Uni

title: Il Comitato europeo per la protezione dei dati (EDPB) e le autorità di protezione dei dati dei paesi e delle organizzazioni che beneficiano di una decisione di adeguatezza dell’UE fanno il punto sui progressi compiuti e definiscono le priorità per il 2027
summary: Bruxelles, 19 novembre - Il CEPD si è riunito il 17 novembre con i commissari e i rappresentanti delle autorità per la protezione dei dati (DPA) dei paesi e dell’organizzazione internazionale destinatari di una decisione di adeguatezza dell’UE. Questo incontro è stato il terzo del suo genere, dopo il primo nell’ottobre 2024 e il secondo nel dicembre 2025 . La riunione è stata un’opportunità per discutere le attività congiunte svolte nel 2026 e individuare la strada da seguire per il 2027. “Le autorità di questa rete sono partner essenziali per il CEPD: insieme possiamo promuovere la privacy e la protezione dei dati su scala globale. L’impegno dimostrato in questa riunione riflette il nostro impegno collettivo ad affrontare le sfide più urgenti della protezione dei dati di oggi. Poiché la tecnologia opera su scala globale, dobbiamo lavorare insieme per affrontare le questioni condivise con cui ci confrontiamo in diverse parti del mondo. Attendo con interesse di continuare e rafforzare la nostra cooperazione.” Presidente del CEPD, Anu Talus Focus per il 2027 La rete ha individuato due temi prioritari per la condivisione delle conoscenze nel 2027: Dispositivi indossabili con particolare attenzione agli occhiali intelligenti Verifica dell’età rispettosa della privacy I partecipanti hanno inoltre concordato di proseguire le discussioni sulla cooperazione nell’attività di enforcement. Contesto Una decisione di adeguatezza è un meccanismo fondamentale della normativa UE in materia di protezione dei dati che consente la libera circolazione dei dati personali dall’Europa verso paesi

title: EDPB and DPAs from countries and organisation with EU adequacy decision take stock of progress and set 2027 priorities
summary: Brussels, 19 November - The EDPB met on 17 November with Commissioners and representatives of the Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) from the countries and the international organisation with an EU adequacy decision. This gathering marked the third of its kind, following the first one in October 2024 and the second one in December 2025 . The meeting was an opportunity to discuss the joint activities carried out in 2026 and identify the way forward for 2027. “The authorities in this network are essential partners for the EDPB: together we can advance privacy and data protection on a global scale. The engagement at this meeting reflects our collective commitment to addressing today's most pressing data protection challenges. With technology operating on a global scale, we must work together to address the shared issues we face in different parts of the world. I look forward to continuing and strengthening our cooperation.” EDPB Chair, Anu Talus Focus for 2027 The network has identified two priority topics for knowledge-sharing in 2027: Wearable devices with a special focus on smart glasses Privacy preserving age assurance The participants also agreed to continue discussing enforcement cooperation. Background An adequacy decision is a key-mechanism in EU data protection legislation which allows free flow of personal data from Europe to third countries or an international organisation offering an adequate level of data protection.* To date, the following countries and international organisation benefit from this: Andorra, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Isra

title: Norwegian DPA fines private individual for credit check and publication of personal data without a lawful basis
summary: Background information Date of final decision: 16/10/2026 National case Controller: Private individual Legal References: Article 6(1) (Lawfulness of processing) Decision: Administrative fine Key words: Legal basis, Fines, GDPR enforcement, Basic principles Summary of the Decision Origin of the case The Data Protection Authority received a complaint from an individual who had been subject to a credit check carried out by a private individual. The individual had access to a credit information service through their work and had used it to carry out a credit check on the complainant for personal purposes. The information obtained from the credit check was subsequently published in various Facebook groups. Key Findings The Data Protection Authority concluded that the credit check was carried out for personal purposes and was unrelated to the work of the individual concerned. The Data Protection Authority therefore concluded that neither the credit check nor the subsequent publication of the information had a lawful basis under Article 6(1) of the GDPR. Decision The Data Protection Authority issued a decision imposing an administrative fine of EUR 940 on the individual for carrying out an unlawful credit check and publishing the information. title: Italian DPA fines Meta EUR 805 million for unlawful access to Facebook users’ photo galleries
summary: Background information Date of final decision: 13/11/2026 National case Controller: Meta Platforms Ireland Limited Decision: Administrative fine, Compliance order Key words: Fines, Online platforms Summary of the Decision Origin of the case The Italian Data Protection Authority (DPA) launched an investigation following a complaint submitted in July 2025 by the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre concerning Facebook's access to users' smartphone photo galleries. The investigation focused on the feature “Get suggestions from your gallery while browsing Facebook”, which displays photos and videos stored on Android devices as suggestions for sharing on the social network. The Authority carried out a technical analysis of the feature and examined whether Meta had obtained valid consent and adequately informed users before accessing information stored on their devices. Key Findings The investigation found that Facebook requested a single system permission to access photos and videos for several different functions. The request was preceded by a generic notice referring to enabling other features, without clearly explaining that access would also enable gallery suggestions. The feature was enabled by default, although it could operate only after system permission had been granted. Once authorised, the app could access the device's multimedia archive on an ongoing basis. The DPA found that Meta had not obtained specific, informed consent for this feature, in breach of Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code. title: Italian DPA fines a company EUR 25 500 over employee access rights and corporate email accounts
summary: Background information Date of final decision: 20/10/2026 National case Controller: Techpartner S.r.l. Legal References: Article 5 (Principles relating to processing of personal data), Article 12 (Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject), Article 15 (Right to access by the data subject),  Decision: Administrative fine, Compliance order Key words: Fines, Basic principles, Data subjects rights Summary of the Decision Origin of the case The Italian Data Protection Authority (DPA) received a complaint from a former employee of Techpartner concerning an inadequate response to a request to access personal data processed during employment. The DPA also examined the company's internal policies governing employees' individual corporate email accounts, including their management after employment ended. Key Findings The company did not respond to the former employee's access request within the deadline required by the GDPR. The company replied only after the DPA opened its investigation, approximately nine months after the request. Its internal rules also allowed former employees' email accounts to remain active for three to six months after termination, with the possibility of reading incoming messages. The DPA found this incompatible with the principles of lawfulness, data minimisation and storage limitation. It confirmed infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), (c) and (e), 12(3) and 15 GDPR. Other allegations concerning video surveillance and occupational medical information did not result in established infringements

summary: Commission preliminarily finds Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act for failure to tackle the sale of illegal products Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:11 The European Commission preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. The Commission preliminarily found that Temu's mitigation measures include ineffective controls to check the compliance of products; a weak content moderation system; and an ineffective sanction system. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: Shopping online should not mean risking the purchase of illegal and unsafe products. Under the Digital Services Act, platforms are responsible for protecting users from the risk of illegal content and goods. summary: Commission hosts Apply AI Summit to boost Europe’s AI innovation and uptake Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 11/16/2026 - 13:43 Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels tomorrow. title: EDPB supports use of other models of contractual clauses for onward transfers of personal data
summary: Brussels 13 November – At its latest plenary, the EDPB adopted a statement on the use of other models of contractual clauses for onward transfers of personal data * . The statement welcomes recent updates made by the European Commission on its FAQs on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) **, recognising that the Model Contractual Clauses (MCCs) developed by the Council of Europe (CoE MCC) and the ones developed by the Ibero-American Data Protection Network (RIPD MCC) may also be used for onward transfers of personal data received under the EU SCCs. Result of a joint work The EDPB and the Commission cooperated closely on this matter. The Board welcomes the Commission’s recognition of these additional instruments to onward transfer personal data received under the EU SCCs. This means that, under the conditions explained in the Commission’s FAQs, an appropriate level of protection of individuals as guaranteed by the European data protection law may be provided when data is onward transferred on the basis of these sets of clauses. In addition, the EDPB statement provides practical guidance to organisations seeking to rely on these MCCs, subject to the conditions set out in the Commission’s FAQs. Note to editors: * Model contractual clauses are contractual clauses developed by organisations and third countries. summary: Bruxelles, 11 novembre – Nel corso dell’ultima sessione plenaria, il CEPD ha adottato una dichiarazione sul primo riesame del funzionamento della decisione di adeguatezza relativa alla Repubblica di Corea e la versione definitiva delle raccomandazioni sulla richiesta di approvazione e sugli elementi e principi che figurano nelle norme vincolanti d’impresa per responsabili del trattamento (BCR-P) . Inoltre, il Comitato ha selezionato il tema della sua sesta azione coordinata di applicazione (MCE). La dichiarazione del CEPD sul primo riesame della decisione di adeguatezza relativa alla Repubblica di Corea si concentra principalmente sulla valutazione delle modifiche apportate al quadro giuridico coreano in materia di protezione dei dati, sia per quanto riguarda gli aspetti commerciali sia per quanto riguarda l’accesso ai dati personali e il loro utilizzo da parte delle autorità pubbliche coreane*. «Il riconoscimento reciproco di norme equivalenti in materia di protezione dei dati tra l’UE e la Repubblica di Corea nel 2025 ha rappresentato un passo importante, che conferma il crescente allineamento tra i due quadri normativi. Accogliamo con favore le modifiche apportate alla legislazione coreana in materia di protezione dei dati, che hanno rafforzato il livello di protezione delle persone fisiche e agevolato il trattamento dei dati da parte dei titolari del trattamento, mantenendo al contempo un livello di protezione sostanzialmente equivalente a quello previsto dal RGPD.» Anu Talus, presidente del CEPD Ad esempio, la legge sulla protezione delle informazioni personali (PIPA)

title: Italian DPA fines Poste Italiane and Deutsche Bank a combined EUR 81 000 for lack of transparency in personal data processing
summary: Summary of the Decision Origin of the case The Italian Data Protection Authority (DPA) received a complaint from an employee of Poste Italiane who, following the rejection of a loan application submitted through BancoPosta, discovered that information concerning her financial situation was accessible through a platform used by authorised company staff. The information included her net income and existing financial commitments. The complainant questioned the disclosure of these data and requested their erasure. The DPA launched an investigation into the processing of personal data by Poste Italiane and Deutsche Bank in connection with the promotion and provision of BancoPosta loans. Key Findings The investigation established that, contrary to their contractual arrangements, Poste Italiane and Deutsche Bank acted as independent data controllers. Poste Italiane collected loan applications and carried out intermediary activities, including identifying financial products suited to applicants' needs, while Deutsche Bank independently assessed creditworthiness and decided whether to grant the loans. The DPA found that the privacy notices provided by both companies did not adequately reflect their respective roles and the personal data exchanged between them. In particular, Poste Italiane had failed to provide sufficiently clear information on the processing carried out during the promotion and distribution of loans, including the recipients of personal data and information flows involving the bank. title: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect
summary: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures. summary: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/26/2026 - 10:28 The European Commission has accepted Temu's action plan to comply with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and tackle the availability of illegal products online. Temu's plan focuses on five measures to remedy its breach of the DSA. The company will carry out a platform-specific risk analysis. It will also use reliable metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the mitigation measures put in place in reducing the risk of dissemination of illegal content. The platform will assess the limitations of its content moderation and analyse whether, and how, its recommender systems may amplify the spread of illegal goods. Additionally, Temu will examine the influence of intentional manipulation and amplification of illegal items, including by sellers exploiting Temu's features to spread potentially illegal listings. The company now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment that covers a six-month period, until 30 November 2026, to ensure the implementation of the measures of the action plan. The action plan is another example of how the DSA is enhancing consumer protection online and limiting the spread of illegal products in Europe. The action plan was submitted following a non-compliance decision in May 2026 , in which the Commission found that Temu had failed to comply with its risk assessment obligations, and issued a €200 million fine. summary: Background information Date of final decision: 2 October 2026 National case  Controller: Xandr Inc. Legal References: Article 6 (Lawfulness of processing), Article 9 (Processing of special categories of personal data) Decision: Administrative fine Key words: Fines, Basic principles, Marketing, Online platforms Summary of the Decision Origin of the case   The case started in 2020 when the Norwegian Consumer Council lodged a complaint against the advertising technology company Xandr (at the time AppNexus, now a part of Microsoft) with the Norwegian DPA (Data Protection Authority). The case concerns real-time bidding in Grindr, a location-based dating app aimed at gay, bi, trans and queer people. Key Findings  The Norwegian DPA has found it proven by clear preponderance of probability that Xandr processed Grindr users’ personal data, at least the fact that individuals were using Grindr, their advertising ID and IP addresses, during real-time bidding. These are personal data under Article 4(1) GDPR and data concerning sexual orientation under Article 9(1) GDPR. Xandr is considered a joint controller for the processing, both as supply-side and demand-side platform. Since the data were special category personal data, explicit consent under Article 9(2)(a) was the relevant legal basis for the processing. Xandr did not obtain consent itself, but relied on Grindr’s consent, which were invalid under Articles 4(11) and 7 GDPR. summary: Point 8(a): AI systems intended to be used to assist judicial authorities or in alternative dispute resolution lobacni Tue, 05/19/2026 - 12:37 (405) Point 8(a) of Annex III classifies as high-risk AI systems intended to be used by judicial authorities or on their behalf to assist a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used in a similar way in alternative dispute resolution. Point 8(a) of Annex III therefore contains two distinct use cases: first, AI systems intended to be used by judicial authorities or on their behalf to assist a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to concrete set of facts; and, second, AI systems intended to be used in alternative dispute resolution (for example intended for arbitration procedures) in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts. title: Point 8 (b): AI systems intended to be used for influencing the outcome of elections or referendum
summary: Point 8 (b): AI systems intended to be used for influencing the outcome of elections or referendum lobacni Tue, 05/19/2026 - 12:37 Overview of use cases and horizontal issues (435) Point (8)(b) of Annex III lists as high-risk AI systems intended to be used for (i) influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or (ii) the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda. That provision clarifies that this use case does not include AI systems the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed to, such as tools used to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view. Recital 62 AI Act explains that the classification of AI systems falling within this use case as high-risk aims to address the risks of undue external interference with the right to vote enshrined in Article 39 of the Charter, and of adverse effects on democracy and the rule of law. (436) For an AI system to be classified as high-risk under the use case listed in point 8(b) of Annex III AI Act, two conditions must be fulfilled: first, the intended purpose of the AI system must be to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or to influence the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda; second, natural persons must be directly exposed to the outputs of the AI system. title: Entry into application of the rules for high-risk AI systems
summary: Entry into application of the rules for high-risk AI systems lobacni Tue, 05/19/2026 - 12:37 (448) According to Article 113 AI Act, Article 6(2) and the corresponding obligations for high-risk AI systems classified under that provision will apply as from 2 August 2026, whereas Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations for high-risk AI systems classified under that provision will apply as from 2 August 2027. These dates are now postponed with the AI Omnibus to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 respectively. (449) Article 111(2) AI Act provides that that act applies to operators of high-risk AI systems that have been placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if, as from that date, those systems are subject to significant changes in their designs. The provision further provides that providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities shall, in any event, take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations for high-risk AI systems by 2 August 2030. Article 111(1) AI Act provides a special regime for AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the legal acts listed in Annex X AI Act which have been placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027. Those systems should be brought into compliance with the high-risk requirements of the AI Act by 31 December 2030. Weight 100

title: Review and update of the high-risk use cases and the Commission guidelines
summary: Review and update of the high-risk use cases and the Commission guidelines lobacni Tue, 05/19/2026 - 12:37 (450) These Guidelines constitute a first interpretation with practical examples of the classification of AI systems as high-risk pursuant to Article 6 AI Act. The AI Office is available to provide additional support to operators and authorities on how to understand the classification of high-risk AI systems and to collect further practical use cases on an ongoing basis with input from providers and deployers of AI systems, the AI Board, and other relevant stakeholders. This will be done through, among others, the AI Act Service Desk on the Single Information Platform 136 and the AI regulatory sandboxes to be established by 2 August 2026. (451) The AI Act also envisages a mechanism to keep the list of high-risk use cases future-proof and to respond to new and emerging risks and market developments. A specific monitoring instrument to evaluate and review, on an annual basis, high-risk use cases listed in Annex III is envisaged by Article 112(1) AI Act. The Commission is also empowered to adopt a delegated act to amend the list in Annex III AI Act by adding new use cases subject to the conditions in Article 7(1) AI Act. It may also amend or remove high-risk AI use cases where both conditions of Article 7(3) AI Act are fulfilled. The Commission may also adopt a delegated act to amend Article 6(3) AI Act by adding new conditions or modifying the existing conditions for the exceptions laid down in that provision.
